lesson.title: Insulated DC: reading the two poles

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the negative's voltage to the hull falling and the positive's rising when you lower the negative's insulation resistance. The two always add to 220 V.
interactive.title: The two poles
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Twelve small screens share one picture, with Back and Continue. Five show an idea and seven ask you to try it. There are no marks and no timers.

The picture shows a 220 V DC board. A battery symbol on the left feeds two bars, the positive pole on top and the negative pole below. Under them runs a thick bar, the hull, which is earth. Two equal detector resistors join the poles to the hull, one on each pole. Each is 100 kΩ. Beside each one, a second resistor stands for that pole's insulation leak. Its label shows its value. At Open it is drawn broken, and at Solid it becomes a plain wire. A voltmeter joins the chosen pole to the hull. On the right, two stacked bars show each pole's voltage to the hull. Together they always fill the 220 V height. Under the hull, a row shows the bridge's alarm lamp, which lights red when the poles are more than 40 V apart. Two lamps, + and −, glow as a simple lamp detector would. Each is as bright as its pole's voltage to the hull ÷ 220. The row ends with the meter's resistance. A thin rule parts it from the key. With its box ticked, an insulation monitor joins the bus to the hull. It has a dial in kilohms with a red alarm line.

The controls sit under the readouts, in rows that wrap on a phone. Two pickers are labelled Positive insulation and Negative insulation. Each offers Open, 500 kΩ, 100 kΩ, 20 kΩ, 5 kΩ and Solid. A picker, Meter on, has two buttons: Positive and Negative. A picker, Meter resistance, offers Ideal, 10 MΩ, 100 kΩ and 20 kΩ. A tick box is labelled Insulation monitor.

The readouts sit in tiles straight under the picture, wrapping onto more rows on a phone. Positive to hull, Negative to hull and Meter reads show volts. Monitor reads shows kilohms.

The rule it computes. Current can leave a pole for the hull only through that pole's paths. It must return through the other pole's paths. So the two sides are in series across the bus, a potential divider with the hull at the tap. Each side's resistance is all its paths in parallel. Call it R_P for the positive and R_N for the negative. R+ is the positive's insulation. In kilohms, R_P = 1 ÷ (1 ÷ 100 + 1 ÷ R+). The meter's resistance is R_m. When the meter sits on that pole, add 1 ÷ R_m inside the brackets. R_N is worked out the same way. Positive to hull = 220 × R_P ÷ (R_P + R_N). Negative to hull = 220 − Positive to hull. So the two always add to 220 V. Open adds no path, and neither does an Ideal meter. Solid makes its side 0. Meter reads shows the voltage of the pole it sits on. The monitor pushes its own small voltage between the bus and the hull. It reads every path in parallel. Monitor reads = 1 ÷ (2 ÷ 100 + 1 ÷ R+ + 1 ÷ R− + 1 ÷ R_m). An Open leak or an Ideal meter adds no term. Its alarm line uses an example level of 100 Ω/V. That puts it at 100 × 220 = 22 kΩ. Below that line, the monitor's lamp turns red.

The opening setting has both poles Open, the meter Ideal on the positive and the monitor off. Each pole reads 110 V and the bridge lamp is dark. Both lamps glow at half brightness. With its box ticked, the monitor reads the two arms alone, 50 kΩ. Now keep the positive Open and put one leak on the negative. A 500 kΩ leak leaves the negative at 100.0 V, and a 100 kΩ leak at 73.3 V. A 20 kΩ leak leaves it at 31.4 V, and a 5 kΩ leak at 10.0 V. A Solid fault leaves it at 0 V. Then the positive's lamp glows at full brightness and the negative's goes dark. The positive reads the rest, in the same order: 120.0, 146.7, 188.6, 210.0 and 220 V. At 500 kΩ the poles are 20 V apart, so the bridge lamp stays dark. It lights from 100 kΩ down. The monitor reads 45.5, 33.3, 14.3 and 4.5 kΩ for the four leaks, then 0 for Solid. With both poles at 20 kΩ, each reads 110 V and the monitor reads 8.3 kΩ. With both poles Open, a 100 kΩ meter reads 73.3 V on either pole. A 20 kΩ meter reads 31.4 V, and a 10 MΩ meter 109.5 V.

Screen 1, show. The opening setting: both poles healthy with insulation Open, no meter loading and the monitor off. The words: "Many DC boards are insulated, with neither pole tied to earth. This 220 V board has a balanced bridge to watch it. Two equal 100 kΩ arms join the poles to the hull, one arm each. The bridge alarms when the poles drift apart. A voltmeter switches between the poles, reading each one to the hull. Each pole reads 110 V, half the bus. Under the hull, two lamps show what a simple lamp detector would. Both glow at half brightness." Read: "A 220 V insulated DC board has a balanced bridge. Two equal 100 kΩ arms join its poles to the hull. Each pole reads 110 V to the hull, half the bus. A lamp detector's two lamps would both glow at half brightness." Still: healthy, both poles Open, meter Ideal on the positive.

Screen 2, try it. "A ship's automation runs on 24 V DC.[^1] Take a 24 V control board with the same kind of detector, two equal arms. Its insulation is healthy. What does each pole read to the hull?" Three choices, in this order: "12 V each"; "24 V each"; "0 V, as nothing is tied to the hull". Right, the first. Hint for the second: "The two readings share the bus between them. Together they make 24 V, not 48 V." Hint for the third: "The detector's arms join each pole to the hull. So the hull sits between the poles." Why: "Equal arms split the bus evenly. Each pole sits 12 V from the hull. The two pole-to-hull voltages always add up to the bus voltage." The picture stays on the healthy 220 V board. Read: the question as it stands.

Screen 3, show. Negative insulation set to 20 kΩ, positive Open. The words: "The negative's insulation falls to 20 kΩ. The pole with less resistance to the hull takes less of the voltage.[^2] Current from the positive reaches the hull through its own paths and returns through the negative's. So the sides form a potential divider, with the hull at the tap. The negative's side is 100 kΩ and 20 kΩ in parallel, 16.7 kΩ. The positive's side is still 100 kΩ, so the sides add to 116.7 kΩ. The negative reads 220 × 16.7 ÷ 116.7 = 31.4 V. The positive reads the other 188.6 V." Read: "With the negative's insulation down to 20 kΩ, its side is 16.7 kΩ. The negative reads 31.4 V to the hull and the positive reads 188.6 V." Still: negative 20 kΩ, positive Open.

Screen 4, try it. "On a 220 V board, the meter reads 189 V on the positive and 31 V on the negative. Which pole has the leak?" Three choices, in this order: "The positive, as it reads high"; "The negative, as it reads low"; "Neither, as the readings add to 220 V". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "A leak lowers its own pole's resistance to the hull, so its share of the voltage falls." Hint for the third: "The readings always add to the bus. The split between them tells you which pole leaks." Why: "The pole with less resistance to the hull takes less of the voltage. The leak drags the negative towards the hull, so the positive climbs. It works like the shifting triangle, with two poles instead of three phases." A right Check sets the negative's insulation to 20 kΩ. Read: the question as it stands.

Screen 5, show. A solid fault on the negative, positive Open. The words: "Make the negative's fault solid. The negative now reads 0 V, and the positive the full 220 V. On the lamps, the positive's glows at full brightness and the negative's goes dark. The board still runs, just as after a first fault on AC. But the hull is now joined to the negative. So a second fault on the positive would short the bus through the hull. A hand on the positive bar and the hull could put 220 V across you. That is well above the 120 V DC safe touch voltage.[^3]" Read: "With a solid fault on the negative, the negative reads 0 V. The positive reads the full 220 V. A second fault on the positive would short the bus through the hull." Still: negative Solid, positive Open.

Screen 6, try it. "A 100 V board has no detector. Its positive leaks 500 kΩ to the hull, and its negative has fallen to 51 kΩ. What does the negative read?" Three choices, in this order: "About 51 V"; "About 90.7 V"; "About 9.26 V". Right, the third. Hint for the first: "The negative takes its own resistance's share of the bus, out of both resistances added." Hint for the second: "That is the positive's share. The pole with less resistance takes less." Why: "With no detector, the two leaks alone make the divider. The negative takes 100 × 51 ÷ (500 + 51) = 9.26 V.[^4] The positive reads the other 90.7 V." The picture returns to the healthy board. Read: the question as it stands.

Screen 7, show. Both poles set to 20 kΩ, the Insulation monitor box ticked. The words: "Damp can lower both poles' insulation together. Set both to 20 kΩ. Each side becomes 16.7 kΩ. The sides are still equal, so each pole still reads 110 V. The bridge sees no imbalance and stays quiet. An injecting monitor tells a different story. It reads every path to the hull in parallel, including the detector's arms. Together they come to 8.3 kΩ, below its alarm line of 22 kΩ. Equal halves mean balanced, not healthy." Read: "With both poles leaking 20 kΩ to the hull, each still reads 110 V. The bridge stays quiet. An injecting monitor reads 8.3 kΩ, below its 22 kΩ alarm line." Still: both poles 20 kΩ, monitor ticked.

Screen 8, try it. "Both poles of a 220 V board read 110 V after a wash-down. Which instrument would show whether the insulation has fallen?" Three choices, in this order: "An injecting insulation monitor"; "The bridge's alarm"; "The voltmeter, switched between the poles". Right, the first. Hint for the second: "The bridge compares the two halves, and they are still equal." Hint for the third: "Equal readings show balance. They say nothing about how low both sides are." Why: "The bridge and the voltmeter both compare the poles. An equal fall on both leaves the halves equal. The monitor pushes its own voltage to the hull and reads the total resistance. So it sees the fall." A right Check sets both poles to 20 kΩ and ticks the monitor. Read: the question as it stands.

Screen 9, show. Both poles Open. The Meter resistance picker set to 100 kΩ, the meter on the negative, then moved to the positive. The words: "Your meter is a path to the hull too. On the negative, it sits in parallel with that arm. Say your meter is 100 kΩ. The negative's side becomes 50 kΩ. It reads 220 × 50 ÷ 150 = 73.3 V, not 110 V. On the positive, the meter pulls that pole to 73.3 V instead. The two readings add to 146.7 V, not 220 V. To show a leak, a detector must add a path to the hull itself.[^5] Every meter adds one too." Read: "A 100 kΩ meter on the negative turns that side into 50 kΩ. The negative then reads 73.3 V, not 110 V. Moved to the positive, the meter reads 73.3 V there too. So the two readings add to only 146.7 V." Still: both poles Open, meter 100 kΩ on the negative.

Screen 10, try it, the first of three mixed puzzles. "A 220 V board has 100 kΩ arms. An old meter reads 31.4 V on the negative, then 31.4 V on the positive. What is going on?" Three choices, in this order: "Both poles have leaked to 20 kΩ"; "The meter itself is a low path to the hull"; "The bus has fallen to 62.9 V". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "Equal leaks would keep the readings equal, but leaks alone never stop the pair adding to 220 V." Hint for the third: "You took each reading alone, and each time the meter dragged its own pole down." Why: "When two readings do not add to the bus voltage, suspect the meter. A 20 kΩ meter turns a 100 kΩ arm into 16.7 kΩ. That side takes 31.4 V. Use a high-resistance meter, and check that the pair adds up." A right Check sets the meter to 20 kΩ on the negative. Read: the question as it stands.

Screen 11, try it. "Two panels are joined into one 220 V system. Each has its own 100 kΩ detector. The negative leaks 20 kΩ to the hull. What does the negative read?" Three choices, in this order: "48.9 V"; "31.4 V, as with one detector"; "15.7 V". Right, the first. Hint for the second: "Both detectors now sit on the same two poles. Their arms add in parallel." Hint for the third: "More detector arms make the leak a smaller share of its side, not a bigger one." Why: "Each side now has two 100 kΩ arms in parallel, 50 kΩ. The negative's side is 50 kΩ and 20 kΩ in parallel, 14.3 kΩ. It reads 220 × 14.3 ÷ 64.3 = 48.9 V. Every extra detector makes the same leak look smaller." The picture shows one panel's detector, with the negative at 20 kΩ. A right Check adds the second panel's detector as a second arm beside each one, and the negative climbs to 48.9 V. Read: the question as it stands.

Screen 12, try it. "On an insulated AC system, a first fault passes a steady current through the cables' capacitance. Now a 220 V DC board's negative has a solid fault to the hull. What flows into the fault?" Three choices, in this order: "A steady current through the capacitance, as on AC"; "A brief charging current, then only what the positive's paths let through"; "Nothing at all, as the board is insulated". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "DC charges a capacitor once. After that, almost no current flows through it." Hint for the third: "The positive's detector arm is still a path to the hull." Why: "The capacitance takes a brief charge when the fault strikes. Once charged, that path carries almost no current.[^6] After that, current runs from the positive through its 100 kΩ arm, then through the hull into the fault. That is 220 ÷ 100,000 = 2.2 mA." A right Check sets a solid fault on the negative. Read: the question as it stands.

Every figure on these screens is an example value, a published figure, or worked from the rule above.
interactive.ignores: The leaks are drawn as fixed resistors. Real insulation changes with damp, heat and voltage. Open means no leak at all. Real insulation never quite reaches that. The battery holds exactly 220 V. The model leaves out the cables' and filters' capacitance to the hull. So every reading changes at once, where a real one would settle. The voltages leave out the monitor's own path to the hull. The bridge's 40 V alarm point and the meters' resistances are example values. The battery's cells and charging are not shown.

explain.text:
On an insulated DC board, neither pole is tied to the hull. Each pole still has a voltage to the hull. The two share the bus voltage between them. The pole with the lower resistance to the hull reads lower.[^2]

Here is why. Current can leave the positive for the hull only through the positive's own paths. Those are its insulation and any detector. With no deliberate earth, it can get back to the negative only through the negative's paths. So the two sides are in series across the bus, a potential divider with the hull at the tap. The same small current flows through both, so each side's voltage is in proportion to its resistance. A pole's voltage to the hull is the bus voltage × its side's resistance ÷ both sides added. Take a 100 V board with no detector. Its positive leaks 500 kΩ to the hull, and its negative has fallen to 51 kΩ. The negative reads 100 × 51 ÷ 551 = 9.26 V, and the positive reads 90.7 V.[^4] A leak pulls its own pole towards the hull, and the healthy pole climbs. It is the shifting triangle again, with two poles instead of three phases. A solid fault puts its pole at 0 V and the other at the full bus voltage.

A detector makes the split easy to read. A [[balanced bridge]] joins each pole to the hull through equal resistors. It alarms when the two halves differ. The simplest detector uses two lamps, one from each pole to the hull. On a healthy bus, both glow at half voltage. Short the negative to the hull, and the positive's lamp glows at full brightness. On a 220 V board with 100 kΩ arms, each healthy pole reads 110 V. Let the negative leak 20 kΩ. Its side becomes 100 kΩ and 20 kΩ in parallel, 16.7 kΩ. It reads 220 × 16.7 ÷ 116.7 = 31.4 V, and the positive reads 188.6 V. But equal leaks on both poles are common on DC boards. Such a [[symmetrical fault]] leaves the halves equal and the bridge quiet. An injecting monitor reads the total resistance to the hull, so it still sees the fault. Every detector or meter is itself a path to the hull. So each one you add moves the readings.

This is a simplified model. It treats every leak as a fixed resistor. It also leaves out the cables' capacitance, which makes real readings settle rather than jump. **On an insulated DC board, the two pole-to-hull voltages add up to the bus voltage. The pole with the lower resistance to the hull reads lower.**

analogy.text: Picture the bus as a potentiometer's track, with the hull as its wiper. The wiper sits where the two sides' resistances put it. With equal arms, it sits in the middle, at half the bus from each end. A leak on the negative lowers the resistance between the wiper and the negative end. So the wiper slides towards the negative end, and the negative's voltage to the hull falls.
analogy.breaks: A potentiometer's track has a fixed total, so turning it trades one side for the other. A leak lowers one side alone, so the total falls too. Real leaks are not fixed resistors either. Damp and heat move them, and the cables' capacitance slows every change.

practice.text:
- Safety first. A floating DC bus is still joined to the hull through its detector and its leaks. Treat each pole as live to the hull.
- Measure each pole to the hull with a high-resistance meter. Then measure pole to pole.
- Add the two pole readings. They should come to the bus voltage. If they fall well short, suspect your meter. It is most likely loading the poles.
- Equal halves mean balanced. That rules out a one-sided leak. It does not rule out an equal leak on both poles. If the board has an injecting monitor, read it too.
- If one pole reads low, that pole is leaking to the hull. The lower it reads, the lower its resistance.
- If one pole reads zero and the other the full bus, the zero pole has a solid fault. Any uneven split short of that points to a partial fault. The bigger the split, the lower the leak.
- With one pole at zero, the other sits at the full bus voltage to the hull. A second fault on it would short the bus through the hull. On a bus above 120 V DC, that pole is past the safe touch voltage.[^3]

**Rule of thumb:** The low pole is the leaky pole. The two readings add to the bus voltage.

**Worked example:** Take a 24 V control board with 10 kΩ detector arms, as an example. The positive reads 4 V to the hull and the negative reads 20 V. They add to 24 V, so the meter is not loading them much. The positive reads low, so it is leaking. Say the negative has no leak, so its side is just its 10 kΩ arm. Each side's resistance is in proportion to its voltage. So the positive's side is 10 × 4 ÷ 20 = 2 kΩ. That is the 10 kΩ arm in parallel with the leak. So the leak is 1 ÷ (1/2 − 1/10) = 2.5 kΩ.

**Common mistakes**
- Blaming the pole that reads high.
- Taking equal halves as healthy insulation.
- Forgetting that your meter is a path to the hull.
- Treating a floating bus as dead to the hull.
- Reading two joined panels' detectors as one. Their arms add in parallel, so the same leak looks smaller.

checks.label: Twelve screens: five that show and seven puzzles, alternating to the ninth and ending on three mixed puzzles
Healthy, the equal 100 kΩ arms put each pole at 110 V, half the bus, with the bridge dark; the monitor reads the two arms alone, 50 kΩ
A negative leak of 500, 100, 20 and 5 kΩ, then Solid, leaves it at 100.0, 73.3, 31.4, 10.0 and 0 V; the positive reads 120.0, 146.7, 188.6, 210.0 and 220 V; the monitor 45.5, 33.3, 14.3, 4.5 and 0 kΩ
A balanced bridge of equal resistors drives its lamp once it becomes imbalanced: dark with equal halves or a 500 kΩ leak (20 V apart), lit from a 100 kΩ leak down
The two pole-to-hull readings add to 220 V at every setting of both leaks and the meter, short of both poles solid
The bus with lower ground resistance has a lower voltage to ground: at every setting, the pole whose side has less resistance reads lower
A bus whose resistance to ground falls to 51 kΩ, against 500 kΩ on the other, reads 100/(500+51)×51 = 9.26 V to ground, and the other 90.7 V
Equal falls hide from the bridge: both poles at 20 kΩ read 110 V each, while the monitor reads 8.3 kΩ, below its 100 × 220 = 22 kΩ alarm line
To give an indication, a detector ends up adding the fault it is trying to detect: every real meter pulls a healthy pole below 110 V
On a healthy board, a 100 kΩ meter reads 73.3 V on either pole (the pair adds to 146.7 V), a 20 kΩ meter 31.4 V, and a 10 MΩ meter 109.5 V
Full voltage on one measurement and zero on the other means a direct short on the side that measures zero
The simplest indicator: both lamps glow with half voltage when healthy; with the negative shorted to the hull, the opposite lamp glows to full brightness
Persons are safe while the touch voltage stays under 120 V DC; a solid fault on the negative leaves the positive 220 V from the hull, above it
Both poles solid shorts the bus through the hull, and the page says so with no number
Worked numbers: 24 V on equal arms is 12 V a pole; 100 ∥ 20 = 16.7 kΩ; two detectors give 50 kΩ a side, 14.3 kΩ with the leak and 48.9 V; 2.2 mA into a solid fault; 62.9 and 15.7 V
The explanation's 24 V board with 10 kΩ arms: a 2.5 kΩ leak on the positive makes its side 2 kΩ, so it reads 4 V and the negative 20 V
Screen 3: as the negative falls through 500, 100 and 20 kΩ, its voltage only ever falls, ending at 31.4 V within 5 s
Screen 7: while both poles fall together, each stays at 110 V all the way, and the monitor ends below its alarm line
Every demonstration settles within 5 s, and a move Dan makes changes the picture in 0.3 s
Before an answer, no puzzle's picture shows its result
The right answer sits first, second or third across the puzzles, never in one place throughout

applied.problem: The worked example's 2 kΩ silently assumes the negative's side is only its 10 kΩ arm; if the negative also leaked, the answer would differ. Also, readings that fall short most likely, not certainly, mean meter loading.

Screen 12's 'its path closes' reads, to anyone who knows circuits, as the path completing and conducting, the opposite of the source's meaning that the capacitive path stops carrying current once charged.
